citation.title: Interval Estimation of Population Means under Unknown but Bounded Probabilities of Sample Selection

standing_assumptions:
Finite-population (design-based) sampling setting; every probability is over the sampling design. Transcribed from the page images of main.pdf (Biometrika 100(1), 235-240; printed page = PDF page + 234). The proof of Proposition 1 is in the Appendix (pp. 239-240, PDF pp. 5-6); the proofs of Lemma 1 and of Propositions 2 and 3 are in the official supplement (staged/supplements/Bka-12-198_supplement.pdf, 2 pp., cited below as 'Supplement p. 1/2').

(S1) Population, sample, ordering, estimand [Section 2, p. 235 (PDF p. 1)]: 'Consider a population $U$ indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$, with associated responses $y_i \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $I_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is sampled from the population; otherwise, let $I_i = 0$. Under a given sampling design, the probability of $i$ being selected is $\pi_i$, so that $\mathrm{pr}(I_i = 1) = \pi_i$. Without loss of generality, assume an index ordering such that the first $n$ units are the sampled units and the remaining $N - n$ are the unsampled units; that is, $I_i = 1$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ and $I_i = 0$ for $i = n+1, \ldots, N$, so that the set of sampled units is $S = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Further, let the units in $S$ be ordered so that $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$. The goal is to estimate the population mean, $\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i/N$.'

(S2) Horvitz-Thompson and Hajek estimators [Section 2, pp. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]: 'When the probabilities of sample selection are known, and if $\pi_i > 0$ for all $i$, then the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of $\mu$, $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (I_i y_i)/(N\pi_i)$, is unbiased. Similarly, we can define a random variable that has expectation 1: $\hat 1_{\mathrm{HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} I_i/(N\pi_i)$. The Hajek (1971) ratio estimator of $\mu$ is then $\hat\mu = \dfrac{\hat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}}{\hat 1_{\mathrm{HT}}} = \dfrac{\sum_{i\in S}\pi_i^{-1}y_i}{\sum_{i\in S}\pi_i^{-1}} = \dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n}$, (1) where $w = (w_1, \ldots, w_n) = (\pi_1^{-1}, \ldots, \pi_n^{-1})$, $y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)$, and $1_n$ is an $n$-vector of ones.'

(S3) Bounded probabilities and the two optimisation problems [Section 3.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 2)]: 'Suppose that we no longer have exact knowledge of the sampling design, instead knowing only that $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ for all $i$. While consistent point estimation is no longer possible without further assumptions, it is possible to obtain an interval estimate for $\mu$. In fact, sharp bounds for the Hajek estimator (1) exist, in the sense that the set of all possible values of $\hat\mu$ is precisely the interval $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}]$. If $\pi_i \in [\alpha, \beta]$, an upper bound on $\hat\mu$ is $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = \max_w\left\{\dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n} : 1/\beta \leqslant w_1, \ldots, w_n \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (2) Likewise, a lower bound is $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \min_w\left\{\dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n} : 1/\beta \leqslant w_1, \ldots, w_n \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (3)' The ratio $\gamma$ is introduced in Proposition 1 (p. 236): 'Let $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ be the relative magnitude of $\beta$ compared to $\alpha$.'

(S4) Brewer scaling [Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]: 'The proposed interval estimator yields asymptotically sharp bounds on $\mu$ itself under the scaling proposed by Brewer (1979) and articulated in Assumption 1.' 'Assumption 1. The sequences of finite populations $\{U_h\}_{h=1}^{\infty}$ and samples $\{S_h\}_{h=1}^{\infty}$ grow as follows. For each $h \geqslant 1$, $U_h = \{U_{h-1}, U\} = \{U, \ldots, U\}$, i.e., $U_h$ consists of $h$ replicates of the original population $U$, so that $|U_h| = hN$. For each $h$, a sample $s_h$ is drawn from $U$ according to the original sampling design, independent of $s_1, \ldots, s_{h-1}$; hence $S_h = \{S_{h-1}, s_h\} = \{s_1, \ldots, s_h\}$. The estimators $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ follow equations (2) and (3), respectively, but applied to the population $U_h$ and the sample $S_h$.'

(S5) Outcome classes, class totals, the limiting optimisation problems [Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]: 'Let $Y$ be the ordered set of distinct outcomes in $U$, so that $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(|Y|)}$, with equivalence classes $\Upsilon_j \equiv \{i = 1, \ldots, N : y_i = y_{(j)}\}$. In the limit of the Brewer scaling, the probabilities $\pi_i$ can be identified up to units with identical outcomes: as $h \to \infty$, $(\sum_{\{i=1,\ldots,Nh : y_i = y_{(j)}\}} I_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{Nh} I_i) \to \Pi_j/(\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k)$ where $\Pi_j = \sum_{i\in\Upsilon_j}\pi_i$. Since $\pi_i \geqslant \alpha > 0$ for all $i$, $Y$ is identified in the limit. If $W_j \equiv |\Upsilon_j|/\Pi_j$ is known for all $j = 1, \ldots, |Y|$, then $\mu$ is identified: $\mu = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j \frac{\Pi_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k} y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\frac{\Pi_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k}}$. However, $W_j$ is actually only identified up to the interval $\beta^{-1} \leqslant W_j \leqslant \alpha^{-1}$; so in the limit, $\mu$ can be identified up to the interval bounded by $\mu_+ = \max_W\left\{\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} : 1/\beta \leqslant W_1, \ldots, W_{|Y|} \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$ (6) and $\mu_- = \min_W\left\{\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} : 1/\beta \leqslant W_1, \ldots, W_{|Y|} \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (7)'

(S6) Assumption 2 [Section 3.2, p. 238 (PDF p. 4)], preceded by: 'By Proposition 2, if $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ as $h \to \infty$, then $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h]$ is asymptotically sharp. A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence.' 'Assumption 2. For any $k \geqslant 0$, $y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$.'

(S7) Reading conventions; these are not printed. They are the ones the validators fixed (validated.json, natural_reading fields) and every target uses them. (a) $n \geqslant 1$, $|Y| \geqslant 1$, and an empty sum is $0$. (b) A rule of the form 'the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ that satisfies [...] $y_{k+1}$' ranges over the integers $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1$, the only $k$ for which $y_{k+1}$ is defined; likewise $0 \leqslant k \leqslant |Y|-1$ for a rule in $y_{(k+1)}$ and for Assumption 2. (c) The objective of (2)-(3) is unchanged when $w$ is multiplied by a positive constant, so with $u = \beta w$ the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$ becomes $[1, \gamma]^n$. For $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n$ write $F^{\mathrm H}_k = \{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{k + \gamma(n-k)\}$ and $F^{\mathrm L}_k = \{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{\gamma k + (n-k)\}$: these are the values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$ at the threshold vectors $w^{k}$ (first $k$ entries $1/\beta$, last $n-k$ entries $1/\alpha$; Appendix, p. 239) and (first $k$ entries $1/\alpha$, last $n-k$ entries $1/\beta$), respectively. The same holds with class totals: for $0 \leqslant k \leqslant |Y|$, $G^{+}_k = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$ and $G^{-}_k = \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$ are the values of the objective of (6)-(7) at the threshold vectors (first $k$ entries $1/\beta$, rest $1/\alpha$) and (first $k$ entries $1/\alpha$, rest $1/\beta$). (d) $\Pi_j > 0$ for every $j$, because each class $\Upsilon_j$ is nonempty and $\pi_i \geqslant \alpha > 0$; hence every denominator in (6), (7) and in $G^{\pm}_k$ is positive. (e) In Section 3.2 the estimators $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ are (2) and (3) computed from the pooled sample $S_h$ (all sampled units of the $h$ replicates); they are defined when $S_h$ is nonempty.

(S8) Transcription notes (checked on 420 dpi crops of the page images). (a) In (5) and in the dichotomous display the left-hand set is printed with $\pi_N$ (capital $N$), although $\hat\mu$ depends only on $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n$. (b) Proposition 3 prints $\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ without hats; the sentence two lines above it and Assumption 1 print $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$. (c) In Proposition 2 the two second sums of the $\mu_-$ display are printed with lower limit $j = k_- - 1$; every other display of the paper has $k+1$ there. (d) The rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$ (p. 236) and the rule for $k_-$ (p. 238, directly below Table 1) are both printed with $\geqslant$; the rules for $k^{\mathrm H}$ and $k_+$ with $\leqslant$. (e) The supplement sets the superscripts H and L in italic and writes $\leq$, $\geq$; the article sets them upright and writes $\leqslant$, $\geqslant$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix, proof of Proposition 1: 'Then $(w^{k+1\prime}y)/(w^{k+1\prime}1_n) - (w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n) \leqslant 0$ implies that ...' (p. 239) and 'Thus $k^{\mathrm H} = \min\{\ldots\} = \min\{\ldots\}$' (p. 240); Supplement, the equivalences with (B1) and (B2): all fail at $\gamma = 1$ with $y = (0, 1)$
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed proof steps refuted.] [Appendix, p. 239 (PDF p. 5)] 'Given the structure of $w^{\mathrm H}$, it remains to show that the optimal objective value of (2) is (4). The first-order condition for $k^{\mathrm H}$ to maximize (2) can be characterized as follows. Let $w^k = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta, 1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$ where the first $k$ entries are $1/\beta$ and the last $n - k$ are $1/\alpha$. Then $(w^{k+1\prime}y)/(w^{k+1\prime}1_n) - (w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n) \leqslant 0$ implies that $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i}{k + \gamma(n-k)} \leqslant y_{k+1}$. If $(w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n) \geqslant (w^{k+1\prime}y)/(w^{k+1\prime}1_n)$, then $(w^{k+1\prime}y)/(w^{k+1\prime}1_n) \geqslant (w^{k+2\prime}y)/(w^{k+2\prime}1_n)$ since $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+2}^{n} y_i}{k+1+\gamma(n-k-1)} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i + (1-\gamma)y_{k+1}}{k+1+\gamma(n-k-1)} \leqslant \dfrac{[k+\gamma(n-k)]y_{k+1} + (1-\gamma)y_{k+1}}{k+1+\gamma(n-k-1)} = y_{k+1} \leqslant y_{k+2}$.' [Appendix, p. 240 (PDF p. 6)] 'Thus $k^{\mathrm H} = \min\left\{k \geqslant 0 : \dfrac{w^{k\prime}y}{w^{k\prime}1_n} \geqslant \dfrac{w^{k+1\prime}y}{w^{k+1\prime}1_n}\right\} = \min\left\{k \geqslant 0 : \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i}{k + \gamma(n-k)} \leqslant y_{k+1}\right\}$. The solution to (3) can be derived in a similar manner.' [Supplement, proof of Proposition 2, pp. 1-2] 'The structure of this vertex solution is of the form $W_+ = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta, 1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$ where the first $k_+ \geq 0$ entries are $1/\beta$ and the last $|Y| - k_+$ are $1/\alpha$. To see this, assume that there exists $\{(W_+)_k, (W_+)_{k+1}\} = (1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$. We will show that replacing the value of the pair with either $(1/\beta, 1/\beta)$ or $(1/\alpha, 1/\alpha)$ will lead to an objective value for (6) that is strictly larger. Define $c_1 \equiv \sum_{j\neq\{k,k+1\}} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}$, $c_2 \equiv \sum_{j\neq\{k,k+1\}} W_j\Pi_j$, and $\mu(W_k, W_{k+1}) \equiv \dfrac{c_1 + W_k\Pi_k y_{(k)} + W_{k+1}\Pi_{k+1}y_{(k+1)}}{c_2 + W_k\Pi_k + W_{k+1}\Pi_{k+1}}$. Then the condition $\mu(1/\beta, 1/\beta) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ is equivalent to $c_2 y_{(k)} - c_1 + \beta^{-1}\Pi_{k+1}(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)}) < 0$ (B1) and the condition $\mu(1/\alpha, 1/\alpha) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ is equivalent to $c_1 - c_2 y_{(k+1)} + \alpha^{-1}\Pi_k(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)}) < 0$. (B2) The assertion is true if either (B1) or (B2) holds. To show this, observe that the sum of the left hand sides of (B1) and (B2) is negative, so at least one of them has to be negative: $\{c_2 y_{(k)} - c_1 + \beta^{-1}\Pi_{k+1}(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)})\} + \{c_1 - c_2 y_{(k+1)} + \alpha^{-1}\Pi_k(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)})\} = (c_2 + \alpha^{-1}\Pi_k + \beta^{-1}\Pi_{k+1})\{y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)}\} < 0$.' [Counterexample from the validator (validate/P025-E004/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3-4); not in the paper.] $N = n = 2$, $(y_1, y_2) = (0, 1)$, $\alpha = \beta = 1$, $\pi_1 = \pi_2 = 1$ (a census). (a) [The hypotheses hold.] $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, $y_1 \leqslant y_2$, and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha = 1$, which Proposition 1 allows ('Let $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$'). (b) $w^0 = w^1 = w^2 = (1, 1)$ and $F_0 = F_1 = F_2 = 1/2$, where $F_k = (w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n)$. (c) [The implication on p. 239 fails at $k = 0$.] Its antecedent $F_1 - F_0 = 0 \leqslant 0$ is true; its conclusion $\{\sum_{i=1}^{0} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=1}^{2} y_i\}/\{0 + \gamma\cdot 2\} = 1/2 \leqslant y_1 = 0$ is false. (d) [The two minima on p. 240 differ.] Over $k \in \{0, 1\}$ (the $k$ for which $w^{k+1}$ and $y_{k+1}$ are defined): $\min\{k : F_k \geqslant F_{k+1}\} = 0$, whereas $\min\{k : F_k \leqslant y_{k+1}\} = 1$ ($1/2 \leqslant 0$ fails at $k = 0$; $1/2 \leqslant 1$ holds at $k = 1$). (e) [Supplement.] The two outcome classes are singletons with $y_{(1)} = 0 < y_{(2)} = 1$ and $\Pi_1 = \Pi_2 = 1$; take $k = 1$, so there are no other classes and $c_1 = c_2 = 0$. The left side of (B1) is $0\cdot 0 - 0 + 1\cdot 1\cdot(0 - 1) = -1 < 0$ and the left side of (B2) is $0 - 0\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1\cdot(0 - 1) = -1 < 0$, but $\mu(1/\beta, 1/\beta) = \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta) = \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\alpha) = 1/2$, so neither $\mu(1/\beta, 1/\beta) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ nor $\mu(1/\alpha, 1/\alpha) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ holds: both printed equivalences fail, and so does the announcement that replacing the pair 'will lead to an objective value for (6) that is strictly larger'. (f) [The results themselves are not refuted.] The box is the single point $(1, 1)$; (2) and (3) both equal $1/2 = \bar y$; the cut point of Proposition 1 is $k^{\mathrm H} = 1$ with $w^{\mathrm H} = (1, 1)$ and (4) gives $(0 + 1\cdot 1)/(1 + 1) = 1/2$; (6) and (7) both equal $\mu = 1/2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)-(S3) of the standing assumptions: the sample $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, the Hajek estimator (1) $\hat\mu = w'y/(w'1_n)$ with $w_i = \pi_i^{-1}$, the bounds $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, the problems (2) and (3) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$, and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ [all p. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]. (S4)-(S5) of the standing assumptions: $Y$, $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(|Y|)}$, $\Upsilon_j$, $\Pi_j = \sum_{i\in\Upsilon_j}\pi_i$, $W_j \equiv |\Upsilon_j|/\Pi_j$, the identity $\mu = \sum_j W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j W_j\Pi_j$, and the problems (6) and (7) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^{|Y|}$ [all p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]. Conventions (S7): empty sums are $0$; cut-point rules range over the $k$ for which the next outcome is defined; $F^{\mathrm H}_k$, $F^{\mathrm L}_k$, $G^{+}_k$, $G^{-}_k$ as in (S7c).
canonical_claim.note: Counterexample to printed proof steps of a Minor finding (P025-E004); priority 3, with its corrected statement P025-T11. Evidence type exact_counterexample, upheld on re-run. It refutes proof steps, not Proposition 1 or Proposition 2: at gamma = 1 the weight box is one point and both bounds are the sample mean.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.2, the sentence before Assumption 2 ('A mild technical condition ... is necessary to guarantee convergence'), Assumption 2 and Proposition 3, corrected: Assumption 2 is sufficient for the printed proof and not necessary; hats restored; index range stated; convergence holds under Assumption 1 alone
canonical_claim.location: p. 238 (PDF p. 4); proof in the Supplement, p. 2
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected passage; the printed one, p. 238 (PDF p. 4), is: 'By Proposition 2, if $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ as $h \to \infty$, then $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h]$ is asymptotically sharp. A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence.' 'Assumption 2. For any $k \geqslant 0$, $y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$.' 'PROPOSITION 3. If Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, then as $h \to \infty$, $\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ almost everywhere.' Sol's smallest repair, validated.json, P025-E005: "Replace 'is necessary to guarantee convergence' with 'is sufficient for the following proof of convergence'; restore hats in Proposition 3; state Assumption 2 for every integer 0 <= k < |Y|. A stronger alternative removes Assumption 2 from Proposition 3 and replaces the fixed-cutoff proof with the uniform-convergence derivation in the artifact."]

(i) [The sentence.] 'A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is sufficient for the following proof of convergence.' (ii) [Assumption 2, with its index range.] For every integer $0 \leqslant k < |Y|$, $y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$. (iii) [Proposition 3, with hats.] If Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, then as $h \to \infty$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ almost everywhere. (iv) [The stronger form, which is what shows that Assumption 2 is not necessary.] PROPOSITION 3 (without Assumption 2). If Assumption 1 holds, then as $h \to \infty$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ almost everywhere.

[Hypotheses of (iii) and (iv) in full.] $U$ is a finite population of $N \geqslant 1$ units with real outcomes $y_i$; the sampling design on $U$ has inclusion probabilities $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ (no assumption on the joint law of the indicators within one sample); $s_1, s_2, \ldots$ are independent samples drawn from $U$ according to that design, and $S_h = \{s_1, \ldots, s_h\}$ (Assumption 1); $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ are (2) and (3) computed from the pooled sample $S_h$; $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ are (6) and (7); 'almost everywhere' is with respect to the joint law of $(s_1, s_2, \ldots)$. Almost surely $S_h$ is nonempty for all large $h$, so the estimators are eventually defined.

(S4)-(S5) of the standing assumptions: $Y$, $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(|Y|)}$, $\Upsilon_j$, $\Pi_j = \sum_{i\in\Upsilon_j}\pi_i$, $W_j \equiv |\Upsilon_j|/\Pi_j$, the identity $\mu = \sum_j W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j W_j\Pi_j$, and the problems (6) and (7) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^{|Y|}$ [all p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]. [Assumption 1, p. 237] as in (S4). [Supplement, p. 2] $P_{h,j} \equiv h^{-1}\sum_{\{i=1,\ldots,Nh : y_i = y_{(j)}\}} I_i$ and (B3)-(B4), transcribed in P025-T21. Conventions (S7): empty sums are $0$; cut-point rules range over the $k$ for which the next outcome is defined; $F^{\mathrm H}_k$, $F^{\mathrm L}_k$, $G^{+}_k$, $G^{-}_k$ as in (S7c).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact statements for each fixed $h$ on which the limit rests (validate/P025-E005/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 4). Write $J = |Y|$, $B = [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^J$, and for $p \in [0, \infty)^J$ with $\sum_j p_j > 0$ and $W \in B$, $f(W, p) = \sum_j W_j p_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j W_j p_j$. (F1) [Class aggregation; (B3) of the Supplement.] Let $C_{h,j}$ be the number of units of $S_h$ with outcome $y_{(j)}$ and $P_{h,j} = C_{h,j}/h$. If $S_h$ is nonempty, then $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h = \max_{W \in B} f(W, P_h)$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h = \min_{W \in B} f(W, P_h)$: the average of the unit weights within a class lies in $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]$, and conversely any $W_j \in [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]$ can be given to every sampled unit of class $j$. Likewise $\mu_+ = \max_{W\in B} f(W, \Pi)$ and $\mu_- = \min_{W \in B} f(W, \Pi)$ by (6)-(7). (F2) [Uniform bound.] With $R = y_{(J)} - y_{(1)}$ and $S = \sum_j \Pi_j > 0$: for every $W \in B$ and every admissible $p$, $|f(W, p) - f(W, \Pi)| \leqslant \dfrac{\gamma R}{S}\sum_{j=1}^{J} |p_j - \Pi_j|$. It follows from the identity $f(W, p) - f(W, \Pi) = \dfrac{\sum_j W_j (p_j - \Pi_j)(y_{(j)} - m)}{\sum_j W_j \Pi_j}$ with $m = f(W, p)$, $|y_{(j)} - m| \leqslant R$ and $1/\beta \leqslant W_j \leqslant 1/\alpha$. (F3) [Extrema.] For real functions $f, g$ on a common set on which both attain their maxima and minima, $|\max f - \max g| \leqslant \sup|f - g|$ and $|\min f - \min g| \leqslant \sup|f - g|$. Hence $|\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h - \mu_+| \leqslant (\gamma R/S)\sum_j |P_{h,j} - \Pi_j|$ and $|\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h - \mu_-| \leqslant (\gamma R/S)\sum_j |P_{h,j} - \Pi_j|$ for every $h$ with $S_h$ nonempty. (F4) [Moments of the replicate counts.] If $X_{r,j}$ is the number of units of class $j$ in the replicate sample $s_r$, then $0 \leqslant X_{r,j} \leqslant |\Upsilon_j|$, $\mathrm{E}X_{r,j} = \Pi_j$, the $X_{r,j}$ ($r = 1, 2, \ldots$) are independent and identically distributed, and $P_{h,j} = h^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{h} X_{r,j}$. (Limit step, not a finite lemma: the strong law of large numbers gives $P_{h,j} \to \Pi_j$ almost surely for each of the finitely many $j$.)

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.2, 'A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence', as printed: a design that violates Assumption 2 and whose estimated bounds equal $[\mu_-, \mu_+] = [5/4, 2]$ for every $h$ on every sample path
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: p. 238 (PDF p. 4)] 'By Proposition 2, if $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ as $h \to \infty$, then $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h]$ is asymptotically sharp. A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence.' 'Assumption 2. For any $k \geqslant 0$, $y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$.' [Counterexample from the validator (validate/P025-E005/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 3, with a Lean check of the arithmetic in artifact/check.lean); not in the paper.] Population of $N = 6$ units with outcomes $(y_1, \ldots, y_6) = (0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3)$. In each replicate, independently select one unit from each of the pairs $\{1, 2\}$, $\{3, 4\}$, $\{5, 6\}$, the two units of a pair being equally likely; replicates are independent. Take $\alpha = 1/4$, $\beta = 1/2$, so $\gamma = 2$. (a) [The standing assumptions and Assumption 1 hold.] Every $\pi_i = 1/2$ and $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$; the replicate samples are independent draws from the same design. $Y = (0, 2, 3)$, $|Y| = 3$, each class has two units, $\Pi_1 = \Pi_2 = \Pi_3 = 1$. (b) [Assumption 2 fails.] At $k = 1$ the first expression of Assumption 2 is $\dfrac{\Pi_1\cdot 0 + \gamma(\Pi_2\cdot 2 + \Pi_3\cdot 3)}{\Pi_1 + \gamma(\Pi_2 + \Pi_3)} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2 = y_{(2)}$. (At $k = 2$ the same expression is $\dfrac{0 + 2 + 2\cdot 3}{1 + 1 + 2} = 2$: the cut points 1 and 2 tie.) (c) [The limiting bounds.] With $W \in [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^3 = [2, 4]^3$, the objective of (6)-(7) is $f(W) = (2W_2 + 3W_3)/(W_1 + W_2 + W_3)$. For every $W$ in the box, with $N_W = 2W_2 + 3W_3$ and $D_W = W_1 + W_2 + W_3$: $4N_W - 5D_W = 3(W_2 - 2) + 7(W_3 - 2) + 5(4 - W_1) \geqslant 0$ and $2D_W - N_W = 2(W_1 - 2) + (4 - W_3) \geqslant 0$, so $5/4 \leqslant f(W) \leqslant 2$; and $f(4, 2, 2) = 5/4$, $f(2, 4, 4) = f(2, 2, 4) = 2$. Hence $\mu_- = 5/4$ and $\mu_+ = 2$. (d) [The estimated bounds, for every $h \geqslant 1$ and every sample path.] The pooled sample $S_h$ has exactly $h$ units at each of the outcomes $0$, $2$, $3$. With unit weights in $[2, 4]$ and class weight sums $A_1, A_2, A_3 \in [2h, 4h]$, the objective of (2)-(3) is $(2A_2 + 3A_3)/(A_1 + A_2 + A_3) = f(A_1/h, A_2/h, A_3/h)$, and every point of $[2, 4]^3$ arises as $(A_1/h, A_2/h, A_3/h)$. Hence $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h = 5/4 = \mu_-$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h = 2 = \mu_+$ for every $h$. (e) [Conclusion.] Assumption 1 holds, Assumption 2 fails, and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ on every path (with equality for every $h$). The condition is therefore not necessary for convergence. This does not contradict Proposition 3, which asserts sufficiency.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected statement; the printed sentences are: (p. 237) 'The proposed interval estimator yields asymptotically sharp bounds on $\mu$ itself under the scaling proposed by Brewer (1979) and articulated in Assumption 1.'; (p. 237) 'However, $W_j$ is actually only identified up to the interval $\beta^{-1} \leqslant W_j \leqslant \alpha^{-1}$; so in the limit, $\mu$ can be identified up to the interval bounded by' (6) and (7); (p. 237) 'PROPOSITION 2. In the limit $h \to \infty$, the bounds $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ on $\mu$ are sharp.' Sol's smallest repair, validated.json, P025-N002, as settled by the doubt check (validate/P025-N002/doubt/doubt.json): 'State: Conditional only on the limiting distribution q_j=Pi_j/sum_k Pi_k of outcomes among sampled units, and with original population size unrestricted, (6)-(7) are sharp lower and upper bounding endpoints, meaning the infimum and supremum of compatible finite-population means. Brewer replication supplies convergence; h-calibrated absolute count rates are not additional identification information. If original N or absolute Pi are retained, the interval is a valid outer bound and sharpness requires the corresponding integer/calibration conditions derived in artifact/derivation.md.']

PROPOSITION 2, first sentence (corrected). In the limit $h \to \infty$, conditional only on the limiting distribution $q_j = \Pi_j/\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k$ of outcomes among sampled units, and with the size $N$ of the original population unrestricted, the bounds $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ on $\mu$ are sharp, in the sense that they are the supremum and the infimum of the means of the finite populations compatible with that information. If $N$, or the absolute limiting totals $\Pi_j$, are also retained, $[\mu_-, \mu_+]$ is a valid outer bound on $\mu$ that need not be sharp.

[Formal content, with every hypothesis; from validate/P025-N002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2-4.] Fix $J \geqslant 1$, reals $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(J)}$, numbers $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ with $\gamma = \beta/\alpha$, and $q = (q_1, \ldots, q_J)$ with every $q_j > 0$ and $\sum_j q_j = 1$. A compatible population is a finite population whose distinct outcomes are exactly $y_{(1)}, \ldots, y_{(J)}$, with $m_j \geqslant 1$ units of outcome $y_{(j)}$ (so $N = \sum_j m_j$ is not restricted), together with inclusion probabilities $\pi_i \in [\alpha, \beta]$ for its units such that $\Pi_j/\sum_k \Pi_k = q_j$ for every $j$, where $\Pi_j$ is the sum of $\pi_i$ over the units with outcome $y_{(j)}$. Its mean is $\mu(m) = \sum_j m_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j m_j$. Let $\mu_+(q)$ and $\mu_-(q)$ denote (6) and (7) with $\Pi_j$ replaced by $q_j$ (the objective of (6)-(7) is unchanged when all $\Pi_j$ are multiplied by one positive constant). Assume that at least one compatible population exists (this is automatic when $\gamma > 1$; when $\gamma = 1$ it holds exactly when $q$ is rational). Then: (a) [Outer bound.] For every compatible population, $W_j = m_j/\Pi_j \in [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]$ and $\mu(m) = \sum_j W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j W_j\Pi_j$; hence $\mu_-(q) \leqslant \mu(m) \leqslant \mu_+(q)$. (b) [Sharpness.] $\inf \mu(m) = \mu_-(q)$ and $\sup \mu(m) = \mu_+(q)$, the infimum and supremum being over all compatible populations. (c) [The box in terms of population proportions.] Let $\mathcal{C}_\gamma(q) = \{r \in \mathbb{R}^J : r_j \geqslant 0,\ \sum_j r_j = 1,\ r_j q_k \leqslant \gamma\, r_k q_j \text{ for all } j, k\}$. The map $W \mapsto r$, $r_j = W_j q_j/\sum_k W_k q_k$, sends $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^J$ onto $\mathcal{C}_\gamma(q)$, so $\mu_+(q) = \max\{\sum_j r_j y_{(j)} : r \in \mathcal{C}_\gamma(q)\}$ and $\mu_-(q) = \min\{\sum_j r_j y_{(j)} : r \in \mathcal{C}_\gamma(q)\}$; and a vector $r$ is the vector of class proportions $(m_j/N)_j$ of some compatible population if and only if $r \in \mathcal{C}_\gamma(q)$ and $r$ has rational coordinates. (d) [Attainment.] $\mu_+(q)$ (respectively $\mu_-(q)$) is the mean of some compatible population if and only if the set of maximisers (respectively minimisers) of $\sum_j r_j y_{(j)}$ over $\mathcal{C}_\gamma(q)$ contains a vector with rational coordinates. (e) [Scope.] When the absolute totals $\Pi_j$ (the limits of $P_{h,j}$ in the Supplement) are retained with fixed $\alpha, \beta$, the compatible class sizes are the integers $m_j$ with $\Pi_j/\beta \leqslant m_j \leqslant \Pi_j/\alpha$, and additionally $\sum_j m_j = N$ when $N$ is known; (a) still holds, and (b) can fail (P025-T16).

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted: p. 237 (PDF p. 3)] 'However, $W_j$ is actually only identified up to the interval $ eta^{-1} \leqslant W_j \leqslant \alpha^{-1}$; so in the limit, $\mu$ can be identified up to the interval bounded by' (6) and (7). 'PROPOSITION 2. In the limit $h 	o \infty$, the bounds $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ on $\mu$ are sharp.' [The reading that is refuted.] In the replication experiment of Assumption 1 the counts of sampled units per replicate are observed, so the absolute class totals $\Pi_j = \lim_h P_{h,j}$ (Supplement p. 2) are part of the limiting information, with $\alpha$ and $ eta$ fixed numbers; 'sharp' then says, at the least, that $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ are the infimum and the supremum of the means of the finite populations compatible with $(\Pi_j)_j$, $\alpha$, $ eta$ (and with $N$, when $N$ is known). A finite population is compatible with $(\Pi_j)_j$, $\alpha$, $ eta$ if it has $m_j \geqslant 1$ units of outcome $y_{(j)}$ and inclusion probabilities $\pi_i \in [\alpha,  eta]$ whose sum over the units of outcome $y_{(j)}$ is $\Pi_j$; this forces $\alpha m_j \leqslant \Pi_j \leqslant  eta m_j$. [Counterexamples from the validators (validate/P025-N002/v1/artifact/derivation.md; doubt/artifact/derivation.md, section 5); not in the paper.] (A) [$N$ not known; integrality.] $U$ has three units with outcomes $(0, 1, 1)$; the design samples each of the three two-unit subsets with probability $1/3$, so every $\pi_i = 2/3$. Take $\alpha = 1/2$, $ eta = 3/4$, $\gamma = 3/2$. (i) The standing assumptions and Assumption 1 (independent replication) hold; $Y = (0, 1)$, $(\Pi_1, \Pi_2) = (2/3, 4/3)$. (ii) (6)-(7) over $W \in [4/3, 2]^2$: $\mu_+ = \dfrac{2\cdot rac43}{ rac43\cdot rac23 + 2\cdot rac43} = \dfrac34$ at $W = (4/3, 2)$ and $\mu_- = \dfrac{ rac43\cdot rac43}{2\cdot rac23 +  rac43\cdot rac43} = \dfrac47$ at $W = (2, 4/3)$. (iii) Every compatible population has $m_1 \in [\Pi_1/ eta, \Pi_1/\alpha] = [8/9, 4/3]$ and $m_2 \in [\Pi_2/ eta, \Pi_2/\alpha] = [16/9, 8/3]$, hence $m_1 = 1$, $m_2 = 2$ and mean $2/3$. (iv) The set of compatible means is $\{2/3\}$, strictly inside $[4/7, 3/4]$: $2/3 - 4/7 = 2/21 > 0$ and $3/4 - 2/3 = 1/12 > 0$. Neither endpoint is the infimum or supremum of the compatible means, although $N$ is not assumed known. (v) Assumption 2 holds: at $k = 0$ both expressions equal $2/3 
eq 0$; at $k = 1$ they equal $3/4 
eq 1$ and $4/7 
eq 1$. (B) [$N$ known; the total-size constraint.] $(\Pi_1, \Pi_2) = (50, 100)$ for outcomes $(0, 1)$, $\alpha = 1/10$, $ eta = 1/5$, $\gamma = 2$, $N = 1000$ (for instance 500 units with $y = 0$, $\pi = 1/10$ and 500 units with $y = 1$, $\pi = 1/5$; $\mu = 1/2$). (i) (6)-(7) over $W \in [5, 10]^2$: $\mu_+ = \dfrac{10\cdot 100}{5\cdot 50 + 10\cdot 100} = \dfrac45$ and $\mu_- = \dfrac{5\cdot 100}{10\cdot 50 + 5\cdot 100} = \dfrac12$. (ii) Compatible class sizes satisfy $250 \leqslant m_1 \leqslant 500$, $500 \leqslant m_2 \leqslant 1000$ and $m_1 + m_2 = 1000$, hence $m_2 \in \{500, \ldots, 750\}$, and every such $m_2$ occurs (choose exactly 50 of the $m_1$ zeros and exactly 100 of the $m_2$ ones uniformly in each replicate: $\pi = 50/m_1$ and $100/m_2$ lie in $[1/10, 1/5]$). (iii) The compatible means are $\{m_2/1000 : 500 \leqslant m_2 \leqslant 750\}$, with supremum $3/4 < 4/5 = \mu_+$: the printed upper bound is not sharp, with gap $1/20$. [What is not refuted.] In both examples $[\mu_-, \mu_+]$ contains every compatible mean (outer bound), and the corrected statement P025-T15, for the information set consisting of the limiting shares only with $N$ unrestricted, holds.
